short: Timur broke the Delhi Sultanate's army and left its capital depopulated for a generation.
full:
Timur crossed the Indus in September 1398, giving as his pretext that the Tughluq sultans were too indulgent towards their Hindu subjects. Before the battle he had the captives taken on the march killed — perhaps a hundred thousand people — on the ground that they could not be guarded while his army was engaged. On 17 December he met Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah and his minister Mallu Iqbal outside Delhi, neutralised their war elephants with caltrops and fire, and destroyed the sultanate's field army. Mahmud Shah fled to Gujarat.

The city surrendered and was then sacked for three days, the killing spreading as attempts to collect ransom turned into house-to-house plunder. Timur left in the new year with the treasury, the elephants and the artisans; the stonemasons among them were set to work on the Bibi Khanym mosque in Samarkand. Delhi was described as empty for two months and took decades to recover. The Tughluq dynasty never did: Timur's governor in Multan, Khizr Khan, took the throne in 1414.
